meta.title: IBM AI-First Transformation Playbook
meta.subtitle: Identify where you need help within the end to end workflow, dive deeper into specific pain points with the modules, and access the full library of examples and templates.
meta.footerText: Created by Claire Liu and Alexandra Ko 2026

endToEndWorkflow.title: End-to-End Workflow
endToEndWorkflow.description: Open Engage, Discover, and Execute to see workflow steps, key activities, readiness checklists, deliverables, modules, and pitfalls.

phaseGroups.name: Engage
phaseGroups.description: Look at the domain as a whole, set up the team and governance (Assess), then narrow to the one workflow worth transforming (Analyze).

steps.name: Assess
steps.subtext: Assess the domain & set up the team
steps.briefDescription: Determine whether the domain is ready by clarifying opportunity, current state, sponsorship, staffing, technical readiness, data quality, and value hypothesis.

keyActivities.title: Conduct current-state assessment
keyActivities.subtext: Gather people, process, technology, data, policies, roles, operating model context, and in-flight transformations.

keyActivities.title: Identify business and technology pain points
keyActivities.subtext: Capture where work is slow, manual, costly, fragmented, risky, low quality, or difficult to scale.

keyActivities.title: Evaluate data readiness
keyActivities.subtext: Confirm required data exists, is accessible, owned, trusted, and usable for AI-enabled transformation.

keyActivities.title: Gather technology architecture blueprints
keyActivities.subtext: Identify systems of record, platforms, integrations, APIs, access constraints, ARB needs, and technical owners.

keyActivities.title: Align stakeholders and executive sponsors
keyActivities.subtext: Confirm sponsor air cover, domain focal, project lead, CIO/BPT/TPT involvement, Finance/EBM support, and decision rights.

keyActivities.title: Set up initial governance and RAID
keyActivities.subtext: Create governance structure, RACI, steering forum, escalation path, and RAID log before the sprint clock starts.

readyToMoveOnChecklist: Current-state people, process, technology, and data context is documented.
Business and technology pain points are stated.
Executive sponsor and domain focal are named.
Initial steering committee and partner organizations are identified.
Key systems, data sources, owners, and architecture constraints are known.
Initial value hypothesis and target workflow are documented.
RAID log is started.

deliverables.title: Current State Assessment
deliverables.description: Captures the domain's people, process, technology, data, operating model, pain points, and readiness baseline. The honest "where we are today" snapshot.

deliverables.title: Business Case Template
deliverables.description: Quantifies the value case tied to the balance sheet or G&A: baseline, target, investment, and ROI.

deliverables.title: Technology & Data Readiness Checklist
deliverables.description: Confirms systems, data sources, owners, quality, access, architecture, and security constraints. Functions as a go/no-go gate before committing.

deliverables.title: Project Charter
deliverables.description: A one-page agreement that scopes the transformation before kickoff: the mandate, value target, sponsor, team, timeline, and sign-off. If you can't complete it, you're not ready to start.

deliverables.title: Business Process Map
deliverables.description: Documents the current-state workflow: handoffs, systems, users, bottlenecks, and automation opportunities.

deliverables.title: Staffing/RACI Matrix
deliverables.description: Clarifies who does what across sponsor, domain focal, PM, product owner, architect, developers, change owner, and value owner — one Accountable per activity.

deliverables.title: RAID Log
deliverables.description: Tracks risks, assumptions, issues, and dependencies throughout the transformation. Reviewed at every steering committee.

steps.name: Analyze
steps.subtext: Narrow down which workflow to focus on
steps.briefDescription: Understand workflows, identify inefficiencies, prioritize opportunities, and define measurable value drivers and technical dependencies.

keyActivities.title: Map current-state business processes
keyActivities.subtext: Document workflow steps, handoffs, user roles, systems, decisions, pain points, manual work, cycle time, volume, and quality issues.

keyActivities.title: Prioritize business processes
keyActivities.subtext: Score opportunities by value, feasibility, data readiness, urgency, user impact, and reuse potential.

keyActivities.title: Define business value
keyActivities.subtext: Translate opportunity into measurable hours saved, cost avoided, revenue influenced, risk reduced, TTR reduced, or quality improved.

keyActivities.title: Analyze workflow bottlenecks
keyActivities.subtext: Identify where AI, automation, data integration, self-service, or redesign can remove friction.

keyActivities.title: Define KPI and measurement strategy
keyActivities.subtext: Define baseline, target, source, owner, cadence, and validation method without overcomplicating the model.

keyActivities.title: Evaluate integration requirements
keyActivities.subtext: Identify source systems, data objects, access paths, technical owners, APIs, architecture review needs, and risks.

readyToMoveOnChecklist: Current-state process map identifies bottlenecks and handoffs.
Candidate workflows are prioritized by impact, feasibility, data readiness, and scale potential.
Baseline, target, owner, source, cadence, and validation method are drafted.
Technical dependency assessment identifies systems, data, integration needs, and owners.
Adoption risks and affected user groups are documented.
Steering committee reviewed major risks and prioritization logic.

deliverables.title: Workflow Analysis Worksheet
deliverables.description: Analyzes bottlenecks, manual work, decisions, user pain, volume, cycle time, technical dependencies, and the AI opportunity for candidate workflows.

deliverables.title: Prioritization Matrix
deliverables.description: Ranks opportunities by value, feasibility, data readiness, urgency, user impact, and scale to select the MVP.

deliverables.title: Measurement Strategy
deliverables.description: Defines baseline, target, source, owner, cadence, and validation method for each metric.

phaseGroups.name: Discover
phaseGroups.description: Plan the AI solution for the chosen workflow: design the future-state, write build-ready requirements, scope the MVP, and set the roadmap.

steps.name: Design
steps.subtext: Design the AI solution, MVP scope & roadmap
steps.briefDescription: Design future-state AI workflow, operating model, MVP scope, governance controls, adoption strategy, technical specification, and reporting model.

keyActivities.title: Design AI-enabled workflows and validate technical feasibility
keyActivities.subtext: Define future-state workflow, AI pattern, user actions, human-in-loop moments, systems, data, and feasibility constraints.

keyActivities.title: Create build-ready requirements
keyActivities.subtext: Translate business need into requirements covering persona, workflow, data objects, systems, acceptance criteria, outputs, and security.

keyActivities.title: Deliver formal roadmap to establish build cadences
keyActivities.subtext: Define MVP, cadence, release plan, out-of-scope items, dependencies, de-scope triggers, and backlog.

keyActivities.title: Establish governance controls
keyActivities.subtext: Confirm decision forums, ARB path, responsible AI, risk controls, escalation thresholds, and owner accountability.

keyActivities.title: Create adoption and change strategy
keyActivities.subtext: Identify affected users, UAT participants, training needs, communications, resistance risks, support approach, and feedback loops.

keyActivities.title: Design reporting model
keyActivities.subtext: Define how KPI, usage, adoption, value, health, and risk data will be captured and reviewed.

readyToMoveOnChecklist: MVP scope, out-of-scope items, and de-scope triggers are documented.
Build-ready business requirements intake is complete.
Technical specification and architecture path are drafted.
ARB, security, privacy, governance, or responsible AI routing needs are known.
Build cadence and sprint backlog are ready.
Adoption, UAT, communications, and support strategy are drafted.
Reporting model reflects MVP scope and metrics.

deliverables.title: MVP Scope Worksheet
deliverables.description: Defines MVP boundaries: in-scope features, out-of-scope items, acceptance criteria, and assumptions.

deliverables.title: Business Requirements Intake
deliverables.description: The build-ready package covering persona, workflow, actions, systems, data, acceptance criteria, technical specification, and solution architecture.

deliverables.title: Workflow Redesign
deliverables.description: A user-perspective future-state journey: how the person's work changes, where AI enters, and where the human stays in the loop.

deliverables.title: Strategic Roadmap
deliverables.description: The roadmap for MVP, pilot, production, scale, backlog, dependencies, cadence, and next releases.

deliverables.title: Change Management Plan
deliverables.description: Plans users, UAT, communications, training, feedback loops, and resistance handling — started early, not at the end.

deliverables.title: SteerCo Charter
deliverables.description: Agenda, attendance, red/yellow/green norms, decision log, escalation rules, and governance structure for running the steering committee.

phaseGroups.name: Execute
phaseGroups.description: Build and experiment to prove feasibility (Build), then scale and sustain what works (Sustain).

steps.name: Build — Experimentation
steps.briefDescription: Configure MVP, run build and UAT cycles, capture KPI and usage data, validate ROI assumptions, manage defects, and decide production readiness.

keyActivities.title: Configure MVP solutions and validate business requirements
keyActivities.subtext: Build against approved requirements, technical spec, user stories, acceptance criteria, and MVP scope.

keyActivities.title: Run sprint cadence and working sessions
keyActivities.subtext: Use standups, demos, steering decisions, blocker reviews, and a practical rhythm such as two-week build plus one-week UAT.

keyActivities.title: Establish test strategy and UAT stakeholders
keyActivities.subtext: Recruit real users, define scenarios, acceptance criteria, feedback format, severity rules, and closure expectations.

keyActivities.title: Capture KPI and usage data
keyActivities.subtext: Instrument MVP to capture usage, adoption, output, workflow volume, deflection, defects, and early value signals.

keyActivities.title: Validate ROI assumptions
keyActivities.subtext: Compare pilot evidence to baseline, target, and value hypothesis; update assumptions when scope changes.

keyActivities.title: Manage defects, blockers, escalations, and de-scope decisions
keyActivities.subtext: Track owners, dates, decisions, and tradeoffs. Surface red items early because red is useful when it triggers action.

readyToMoveOnChecklist: MVP is built against approved requirements and technical spec.
UAT strategy, users, scenarios, and acceptance criteria are active.
KPI and usage data are being captured.
ROI assumptions are reviewed against pilot evidence.
Defects, blockers, and escalations are tracked with owners and dates.
De-scope decisions are documented and communicated.
Production readiness decision is documented.

deliverables.title: Sprint Cadence Plan
deliverables.description: The operating cadence for build, standups, working sessions, UAT cycles, decisions, and steering reviews

deliverables.title: UAT Feedback Tracker
deliverables.description: Tracks real-user testing feedback, defects, severity, acceptance criteria, priority, ownership, and resolution.

deliverables.title: Pilot Results
deliverables.description: A reference readout covering MVP scope, users tested, outcomes, UAT feedback, defects, adoption, and evidence.

deliverables.title: ROI Analysis
deliverables.description: A reference comparing ROI assumptions against pilot evidence, usage analytics, workflow impact, and validated value.

deliverables.title: Usage Analytics
deliverables.description: Reference analytics for active users, repeat users, workflow volume, deflection, and usage events.

deliverables.title: Production Readiness Packet
deliverables.description: Confirms requirements, UAT results, defects, limitations, support path, risks, and the go/no-go for scale.

steps.name: Sustain — Scale & Adopt
steps.briefDescription: Operationalize solution, monitor adoption and value, complete graduation, define ownership, scale successful patterns, and manage continuous improvement.

keyActivities.title: Monitor adoption and utilization
keyActivities.subtext: Track active users, repeat users, workflow volume, deflection, feedback, support needs, and operational integration after launch.

keyActivities.title: Track realized business value
keyActivities.subtext: Validate realized value against baseline and target using Finance, EBM, operational data, or approved reporting sources.

keyActivities.title: Conduct KPI reviews
keyActivities.subtext: Review value, adoption, performance, support, and risk metrics on a defined cadence with owners who can act.

keyActivities.title: Complete graduation and ownership handoff
keyActivities.subtext: Confirm business, technical, prompt/content, support, and value ownership. Graduation means ownership-ready, not demo-complete.

keyActivities.title: Scale successful patterns
keyActivities.subtext: Identify expansion to more users, workflows, domains, geographies, or Client Zero proof points.

keyActivities.title: Define continuous improvement strategy
keyActivities.subtext: Assign backlog ownership, support model, technical maintenance, prompt/content updates, and next-release roadmap.

readyToMoveOnChecklist: Business, technical, support, value, and prompt/content owners are named.
Graduation checklist is complete.
Support and maintenance model is documented.
KPI dashboard and value reporting cadence are live.
Adoption and utilization are monitored after launch.
Scaling recommendations and reusable patterns are documented.
Continuous improvement backlog and next-release roadmap have an owner.

deliverables.title: Graduation Checklist
deliverables.description: Confirms MVP acceptance, owners, support model, telemetry, value tracking, and adoption plan before declaring done.

modules.title: Modules
modules.description: Modules are pain-point deep dives organized by lifecycle step.

chapters.title: Value Measurement & ROI
chapters.definition: AI-first transformation value must be defined before the solution is built and validated after the solution is adopted. This chapter helps domain leads move from a high-level value hypothesis to a measurable business case, then from pilot evidence to realized value reporting. The goal is not to create a complex finance model; the goal is to define a simple, credible, repeatable way to prove whether the transformation improved the workflow.

keyPrinciples: Hard line savings > soft benefits (cost avoidance doesn't count)
Baseline collection must start day 1 (not after the pilot)
Lightweight and finance-blessed (not complex models)
Tied to IBM's balance sheet or G&A reduction
3-5 leading indicators (not 20 metrics)
Weekly tracking during pilot, monthly after launch
escalationPaths: Finance/EBM validation issues → Domain CFO or EBM lead
Baseline data access issues → Domain data owner or IT
Target setting disputes → Domain executive sponsor
Value realization gaps → Steering committee
successCriteria: Business case approved by finance/EBM
Baseline and target metrics defined and validated
Pilot shows early value signals (even if not at full target)
Production solution has auto-instrumentation for metrics
Post-launch value is tracked and reported monthly
Lessons learned are documented and scaled

commonPitfalls: Starting with soft benefits or cost avoidance instead of hard line savings
Using estimates instead of actual baseline data from source systems
Waiting until after the pilot to define metrics
Creating complex finance models instead of lightweight tracking
Not getting finance/EBM validation early
Defining too many metrics instead of focusing on 3-5 leading indicators

example.title: Speaker Agent Success
example.description: The MCC Event Speaker Agent team defined baseline metrics during the Analyze phase by measuring the current manual process: average time to identify and confirm speakers (5 days), number of back-and-forth emails (12 per event), and speaker confirmation rate (65%). They set clear targets: reduce time to 2 days, reduce emails to 3, increase confirmation rate to 85%. Finance validated the approach by confirming the metrics tied to G&A reduction through improved event planning efficiency. The team tracked these metrics weekly using a simple spreadsheet linked to their event management system.

example.title: Bob Agent ROI Validation
example.description: During the Build phase, the Bob Agent team instrumented the solution to automatically track usage, response time, and user satisfaction. They discovered that while usage was high (85% adoption), the time savings were lower than expected (20% vs. 40% target) because users were still manually validating Bob's outputs. The team surfaced this "red" finding to the steering committee, adjusted the target to 25%, and added a confidence score feature to reduce manual validation. By the end of the pilot, they hit the adjusted target and had credible evidence for the production readiness decision.

example.title: Manufacturing Transformation Value Realization
example.description: After launching an AI-powered system integration solution, the Manufacturing domain tracked value realization for 6 months through their EBM dashboard. They achieved a 40% reduction in system integration time and 30% improvement in data processing efficiency, exceeding their targets. However, they discovered that only 60% of eligible workflows had adopted the solution. By addressing adoption barriers (training, change management, process updates), they increased adoption to 85% and realized an additional 15% in value. They documented the lessons learned and scaled the pattern to 3 other manufacturing sites, multiplying the value impact.

chapters.title: Prioritization & Roadmap
chapters.definition: Select workflow opportunities, scope realistic MVPs, sequence delivery, and maintain a scalable roadmap. This chapter helps domain leads move from a broad set of AI possibilities to a focused, sequenced delivery plan. The goal is not to build a perfect long-term roadmap; the goal is to make smart decisions about what to build first, what to defer, and when to pivot based on learning.

keyPrinciples: Value over excitement (prioritize by business impact, not AI novelty)
MVP mindset (ship working software in 8-12 weeks, not 6 months)
De-scope is a feature (cutting scope to hit timeline is success, not failure)
Data readiness drives feasibility (no data = no MVP)
User adoption > technical perfection (working solution beats elegant architecture)
Roadmap is a living document (update quarterly based on results)
escalationPaths: Scope disputes or feature creep → Product owner or domain sponsor
Timeline conflicts or resource constraints → AIFT orchestration lead or PMO
Prioritization disagreements → Domain executive sponsor or steering committee
Technical feasibility blockers → CIO/BPT architect or platform team
successCriteria: Prioritization criteria are clear and consistently applied
MVP scope is locked before build starts (with agreed de-scope triggers)
Roadmap shows next 2-3 releases with clear sequencing rationale
Stakeholders understand what's in, what's out, and why
De-scope decisions are made quickly when blockers emerge
Post-launch results inform next prioritization cycle

example.title: MCC Event Planning Prioritization
example.description: The MCC team had 15 potential AI opportunities across event planning workflows. Instead of building all of them, they used a prioritization matrix to evaluate each opportunity on value (time savings, cost reduction), feasibility (data availability, system integration), and readiness (user willingness, sponsor support). The Speaker Agent emerged as the top priority because it addressed the highest-pain workflow (5 days to find speakers), had readily available data (speaker database, event history), and had strong executive sponsorship. The team documented why the other 14 opportunities were deferred, creating a clear roadmap for future releases. This disciplined prioritization allowed them to ship a working MVP in 10 weeks instead of spreading resources across multiple half-built solutions.

chapters.title: Systems Integration
chapters.definition: Translate business needs into build-ready requirements and connect AI capabilities with systems, data, architecture, and support models.

keyPrinciples: CIO/BPT integration starts at Analyze (not after design is done)
ARB process must be understood and scheduled early (not assumed)
Technical specifications must be build-ready (not high-level concepts)

example.title: Event Briefer Agent Change Strategy Success
example.description: The Event Briefer Agent team designed their change strategy during the Design phase by identifying 3 user segments: event planners (high volume, low complexity), executive assistants (low volume, high stakes), and marketing coordinators (medium volume, content-focused). They recruited 2 UAT users from each segment to ensure the solution worked for all workflows. The team created a communication plan that explained how the agent would reduce the 4-hour brief creation process to 30 minutes, addressing the 'what's in it for me' question directly. Instead of classroom training, they designed workflow-embedded job aids and tooltips that appeared at key decision points. They also planned listening sessions to surface resistance early and adjust the solution based on feedback. By designing for adoption from the start, they achieved 75% adoption within 2 weeks of launch.

example.title: Speaker Agent Sustained Adoption Success
example.description: After launching the Speaker Agent, the MCC team tracked adoption metrics weekly and discovered that while 85% of event planners had tried the agent, only 60% were using it consistently. Through listening sessions, they identified 3 adoption barriers: (1) users didn't trust the agent's speaker recommendations, (2) the workflow required too many manual validation steps, and (3) training materials didn't cover edge cases. The team addressed these barriers by adding a confidence score to recommendations, streamlining the validation workflow, and updating training with real examples. They also created a 'Speaker Agent Champions' program where early adopters shared success stories and tips. Within 8 weeks, consistent usage increased to 80%, and the team documented the adoption playbook to scale to other MCC workflows. The key lesson: adoption is not a one-time event, it's a continuous process of listening, improving, and reinforcing.

caseStudy.title: Full Journey: From Identifying a Workflow to 90 Day AI MVP
caseStudy.subtitle: How a domain team uses the AIFT workflow to discover the right use case, test feasibility, build a 90-day MVP, and scale what works.
caseStudy.overview: This composite journey shows the transformation process in action. The team does not begin with a fixed solution. The team starts with a domain mandate, identifies candidate workflows, prioritizes the best MVP, tests riskiest assumptions, and uses project-management discipline to move from pilot to production.
caseStudy.startingContext: Marketing leadership wants to reduce manual effort, cycle time, and inconsistent execution across event-related workflows. Leaders know event planning, executive brief creation, speaker coordination, campaign content reuse, and post-event reporting are all pain points, but the best first AI use case is not yet known.
caseStudy.navInstruction: Click through each phase below to follow the team's journey from mandate to scaled MVP.

phases.mindset: We have a domain transformation mandate, but we don't yet know the right use case.
phases.summary: The team looks at the marketing/events domain as a whole: clarifies the mandate, confirms sponsorship, stands up the team and governance, and takes an honest read on technology and data readiness.
keyActions: Clarify the transformation mandate and what leadership expects
Identify candidate workflow areas worth transforming
Confirm the executive sponsor and domain focal
Set up the RACI and stand up the steering committee
Start a current-state assessment of the candidate workflows
Review technology and data readiness at a high level
Draft an initial value hypothesis
takeaways: Do not start build until sponsor, focal, technical owner, value owner, and change owner are named
Use data readiness as a go/no-go input
Start RAID immediately
Resist jumping to solution before understanding the problem space

sideways.issue: Sponsor wants to jump directly to 'build an event agent.'
sideways.howHandled: Domain focal reframes the work: 'We are not choosing the agent yet. We are choosing the workflow opportunity first.' The team commits to a short Analyze phase to compare candidate workflows.

weeks.label: Mandate and team
did: Marcus met with Dana to translate the broad mandate ('reduce manual effort in events') into a scoped engagement charter
Named the core team: product owner, architect, value owner, change owner, two event SMEs
Stood up the steering committee and set a biweekly cadence with Dana chairing
Opened the RAID log and the shared Box project folder on day one

blocker.issue: Dana pushed to 'just build an event agent' in the kickoff and skip discovery.
blocker.handled: Marcus reframed it: 'We're choosing the workflow opportunity first, not the agent.' He committed to a 2-week Analyze phase and a decision gate, which Dana accepted because it came with a date.

weeks.label: Current-state assessment
did: Ran a current-state assessment across five candidate event workflows
Walked the technology and data readiness checklist with Sofia to flag access gaps early
Drafted a first value hypothesis with Tom: target a workflow worth at least 1,000 analyst-hours/year
Confirmed sponsor, focal, technical owner, value owner, and change owner are all named before exiting Engage

phases.mindset: Which single workflow should we transform first, and why?
phases.summary: The team maps the candidate event workflows, validates pain with users, scores them on value and feasibility, and commits to one MVP target: speaker recommendations + event brief drafting.
keyActions: Map the candidate event workflows end to end
Validate the real pain points directly with users
Score candidates on value, feasibility, data readiness, and adoption
Define baseline metrics for the top candidates
Prioritize and commit to the MVP workflow

comparison.dataStatus: Data exists but quality is uneven
Lower user pain compared with pre-event work

phases.mvpDecision: MVP = speaker recommendations + event brief draft
phases.mvpRationale: This combination has high user pain, measurable cycle-time reduction, available data, and a clear adoption path.

baseline.speakerIdentification: 5 days to identify and confirm speakers
baseline.briefCreation: 4 hours to draft an executive event brief

target.speakerIdentification: 2 days to identify and confirm speakers
target.briefCreation: 45 minutes to draft an event brief

takeaways: Score opportunities by value, feasibility, data readiness, and adoption
Pick the smallest useful MVP
Define metrics before you design
Use data readiness to inform the choice

sideways.issue: Narrative generation is the most exciting idea, but dependency assessment shows content ownership and data access are not ready.
sideways.howHandled: The team moves narrative generation to next-release backlog and keeps the MVP focused.

phases.mindset: What exactly are we building for this workflow, and can we build it?
phases.summary: The team plans the AI solution for the chosen workflow: redesigns the future-state from the user's perspective, writes build-ready requirements, scopes the MVP, sets the roadmap, and plans adoption from the start.
keyActions: Redesign the future-state workflow from the user's perspective
Write build-ready business requirements with the architect
Scope the MVP — explicitly in and explicitly out
Set the roadmap: MVP → pilot → scale
Plan adoption, UAT users, and training now
takeaways: Design around the user outcome, not the existing process
Make requirements build-ready, not conceptual
Recruit real UAT users before the build starts
Plan change management from day one

sideways.issue: The first requirements package was too conceptual for CIO/BPT to build from.
sideways.howHandled: The team revised it into a build-ready package with data objects, source systems, named owners, acceptance criteria, a fallback path, and telemetry requirements. It was approved on the second pass.

phases.mindset: How do we keep delivery moving while learning from real users?
phases.summary: Runs 30-day feasibility experiment, then builds MVP in 2-week sprints, runs UAT with real users, tracks metrics weekly, manages defects/blockers, uses steerco for decisions, de-scopes lower-value work, and prepares production readiness evidence.
keyActions: Run the 30-day learn-fast feasibility experiment first
Test the riskiest assumptions: data, process, technology
Hit the Continue / Pivot / Abandon decision gate
Build the MVP in 2-week sprints
Run UAT with real users every sprint
Track metrics, defects, and blockers weekly
Use the steering committee to clear blockers and decisions
De-scope lower-value work to protect the timeline
Prepare production-readiness evidence
takeaways: UAT is an adoption mechanism, not just a testing phase
Red items should be surfaced early with detailed one-pagers
ROI assumptions must be updated when scope changes
Trust and explainability are adoption drivers
De-scope is a success behavior when timeline or data reality changes

sideways.issue: UAT users do not trust recommendations
sideways.howHandled: Add recommendation rationale, confidence indicator, source links, and feedback flag
Assign data owner, document quality issues, add data validation step
Escalate to steerco with red-item one-pager, de-scope formatting features to protect core MVP

operatingRhythm: UAT board for feedback, bugs, enhancements
Apptio roadmap / Monday / Jira / Box / Slack or Teams as source of truth
evidence: 72% of UAT users completed speaker shortlisting using the assistant
Speaker shortlist time reduced from 5 days to 2.5 days
Event brief draft time reduced from 4 hours to 70 minutes
Recommendation explainability became top improvement theme

weeks.label: Feasibility experiment begins (Days 1–30)
did: Kicked off the 30-day learn-fast feasibility experiment to test the riskiest assumptions before committing to a full build
Set three test criteria: data access granted, data quality sufficient, brief quality meets a minimum threshold
Daily standups under 30 minutes; workstreams tracked in Apptio and Monday

weeks.label: Data quality scare
did: Connected to the speaker and event data sources and ran the first quality assessment
Found the speaker data was inconsistent enough to threaten recommendation accuracy

blocker.issue: Data quality was worse than the readiness checklist suggested and threatened the whole value story.
blocker.handled: Tom and Sofia assigned a data owner, documented the specific quality issues, and added a data-validation step to the pipeline. The fix held — but it cost most of week 7.

weeks.label: Feasibility decision gate
did: Reviewed feasibility evidence against the three criteria at the Continue / Pivot / Abandon gate
All three cleared; steering committee approved moving into the build sprints
Updated the ROI model with real development cost inputs from Apptio

weeks.label: Sprint 1 — core build
did: Built the speaker-shortlist engine and the first brief-draft generator in a 2-week sprint
Ran the first UAT round with real event planners, not managers
Tracked metrics, defects, and blockers weekly; reviewed RAID at sprint end

weeks.label: Trust problem surfaces in UAT
did: UAT users were hesitant to act on the AI's speaker recommendations
Identified explainability as the top improvement theme from feedback

blocker.issue: UAT users didn't trust the recommendations, which would have killed adoption regardless of accuracy.
blocker.handled: The team added recommendation rationale, a confidence indicator, source links, and a feedback flag. Trust — and usage — climbed in the next round.

weeks.label: Sprint 2 — refine and instrument
did: Shipped the explainability features and refined brief quality based on UAT
Instrumented the workflow telemetry so value could be tracked automatically
Pilot evidence: 72% of UAT users completed shortlisting with the assistant; brief draft time down from 4 hours to 70 minutes

weeks.label: Integration dependency slips
did: A connector/API the brief generator depended on slipped its delivery date
Raised it at steering committee with a detailed red-item one-pager

blocker.issue: A connector/API dependency slipped and threatened the production timeline.
blocker.handled: Marcus escalated at steerco with a one-pager and de-scoped the brief-formatting niceties to protect the core MVP. Dana cleared the dependency through the partner team within the week.

weeks.label: Sprint 3 — production readiness
did: Hardened the MVP, closed or accepted all open defects, and completed back-testing
Assembled production-readiness evidence for the go/no-go decision
Confirmed security, legal, and compliance approvals before go-live

phases.mindset: How do we make sure this does not die after the sprint?
phases.summary: Completes graduation checklist, confirms business/technical/support/prompt-content/value owners, monitors adoption and value, addresses adoption barriers, builds next-release backlog, captures Client Zero proof point, and scales pattern.
keyActions: Complete the graduation checklist
Confirm business, technical, support, content, and value owners
Monitor adoption and value against baseline
Identify and address the top adoption barriers
Build the next-release backlog
Capture the Client Zero proof point
Recommend where to scale the pattern next
takeaways: Graduation means ownership-ready, not demo-complete
Adoption must be managed after launch
Value realization should drive scaling decisions
Champions and office hours accelerate adoption

sideways.issue: Adoption plateaued because some users kept using old templates and manual channels.
sideways.howHandled: The team routes new requests through the AI-enabled workflow, creates office hours, updates training, names champions, adds edge-case examples, and monitors adoption weekly.

evidence: 80% consistent usage among target users after 8 weeks
Speaker shortlist cycle time reduced from 5 days to 2 days
Event brief draft time reduced from 4 hours to 45 minutes
Top three adoption barriers documented and addressed
Pattern recommended for expansion to narrative generation and executive briefing workflows

weeks.label: Graduation and ownership
did: Completed the graduation checklist — ownership-ready, not just demo-complete
Confirmed business, technical, support, prompt/content, and value owners by name
Stood up the KPI dashboard and value-realization reporting against baseline

weeks.label: Adoption and scale
did: Monitored adoption weekly; after 8 weeks, 80% of target users were using it consistently
Speaker shortlist cycle time landed at 2 days (from 5); brief draft at 45 minutes (from 4 hours)
Captured the Client Zero proof point and recommended scaling the pattern to narrative generation and exec briefing

blocker.issue: Adoption plateaued because some users kept using old templates and manual channels.
blocker.handled: The team routed all new requests through the AI-enabled workflow, ran office hours, refreshed training, named champions, and added edge-case examples. Adoption climbed past 80%.
